name: Olga Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Olga. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work nights, mostly, for a fit-out firm that does shops and offices. This month it's a phone shop and a coffee place in the shopping centre, so we go in at nine when the shutters come down and work till five in the morning. I'm on stud walls and ceilings, which means putting up the metal frames and boards that make the rooms inside a building, and I'm learning the joinery for counters. I'm the junior on a crew of five, under a woman called Gloria who's been doing this since she was sixteen. I like the quiet of an empty shopping centre at three in the morning, and I don't like the drive home when everyone else is going to work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ran housekeeping at a big hotel for twenty-two years. They brought in the app check-in and those little robot hoovers, cut the team in half, and I didn't fancy being the one who told my girls they were out. So I left on my own terms. My husband Pavel and I have a small flat we rent out, and the house is nearly paid, so I had room to try something new, and fit-out pays well at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, people can stop panicking. I'd probably say it to the girls in the WhatsApp group from the hotel, because half of them lost their jobs over the robot hoovers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I just keep learning my trade. I use the chat thing now and then to help write messages to our tenant, because I'm not good with polite letters. On site, it changes nothing at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep going with Gloria, get better at the counter joinery, maybe ask for some day work in the summer so I see the sun. Keep paying a bit extra off the mortgage so it's done before I'm sixty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. Normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of the trade for you right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting a ceiling grid level across a big room. Gloria does it by eye and a laser, and I still end up with a dip in the corner. She makes me take it down and do it again, which I hate, but she's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the robot hoovers. What was that like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strange, honestly. They were slow and they got stuck under the beds, and the girls had to rescue them. But the bosses had already done the sums, so it didn't matter that they were rubbish.

S0.say: I'd say good, people can stop panicking. I'd tell my old hotel colleagues on WhatsApp, because half of them lost jobs over the robot hoovers.
S0.think: Privately, I'd just keep learning my trade. I use the chat app now and then for polite messages to our tenant, but on site it changes nothing.
S0.do: Keeps working with Gloria and focuses on counter joinery, and may ask for summer day work. Pays extra off the mortgage to clear it before she turns sixty.
S0.quote: They were slow and they got stuck under the beds, and the girls had to rescue them. But the bosses had already done the sums
S0.fieldNote: Olga's lesson from the hotel is sharp: machines don't have to be good to replace people if the bosses have done the sums. She uses AI only for things she finds awkward, like letters. Her current struggle is concrete: levelling a ceiling grid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be hard for some, fine for others, and we need to get people retrained properly. I'm not one for big opinions online, I'd say it at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think fit-out is mostly safe for a while, every shop is different and the buildings are never square. What worries me is Pavel, he drives a taxi, and that's exactly the kind of job this goes after. I'd be fine. I'm not sure he would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the drawing apps the bigger fit-out firms use, once Gloria or the boss had tried them. I'd put more aside each month, maybe two hundred extra, in case Pavel's fares drop. And I'd talk to him about whether he wants to do a course in something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More for him than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that talk with Pavel be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over dinner on a Sunday, when I'm not on nights. He'd say, Olga, people will always want a driver who knows the back roads. And I'd say, that's what I said about my girls and the hoovers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you watch first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rental flat's mortgage, it's the one with the bigger payment. If Pavel's money dropped, I'd want to know we could cover that from my wages alone. I think we could, just about.

S1.say: I'd say it'll be hard for some and fine for others, and people need proper retraining. I'm not one for big opinions online, so I'd say it at home.
S1.think: Off the record, I think fit-out is safe for a while because every shop is different. My worry is my husband, a taxi driver, which is exactly the sort of job this targets.
S1.do: Starts using the drawing apps bigger fit-out firms use once her boss has tried them, and saves about two hundred extra a month. Talks to her husband about retraining.
S1.feel: Uneasy, more for her husband than for herself.
S1.quote: He'd say, Olga, people will always want a driver who knows the back roads. And I'd say, that's what I said about my girls and the hoovers.
S1.fieldNote: Her own trade feels safe to her because no shop is square, so the worry moves to Pavel's taxi. She uses the hotel story to push back on his confidence. She checks whether her wages alone could cover the rental flat's mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and someone in charge has to make it fair, and I don't much care which party does it. People need money while they work out what to do. I'd sign whatever petition was going round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be in trouble on two fronts. Pavel's taxi would go first, and then a robot that can fix boards to a ceiling all night without a break would get my job. Our tenant might lose their job too and stop paying, so even the flat isn't safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, I'd talk to Pavel about selling the rental flat while prices are still decent, and putting the money where we could reach it. I'd stop the extra mortgage payments and keep the cash. When it hit, I'd look for whatever work was left, maybe managing the people who look after the robots, since I managed a team for twenty-two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Busy-anxious, though, not frozen. I'd be making lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's at the top of that list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ring the estate agent. Then sit down with Pavel and the bank statements. Then ring my daughter Lena, who's a hairdresser, and tell her she might be all right, people still want a person with scissors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've talked a lot about lists. What would you be doing the night it really sinks in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably standing in a dark shopping centre at three in the morning, holding a board up, thinking, this might be my last job like this. Gloria would tell me to stop daydreaming and get the screws in.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and whoever's in charge has to make it fair, whatever the party. People need money while they work things out, and I'd sign the petition.
S2.think: Between us, I'd be hit twice: my husband's taxi first, then a robot fixing boards all night would take my job. Our tenant might stop paying too, so even the flat isn't safe.
S2.do: Talks with her husband about selling the rental flat while prices hold and stops extra mortgage payments to keep cash. Looks for work supervising the people who maintain the robots, using her management years.
S2.feel: Anxious but busy, making lists rather than freezing.
S2.quote: Standing in a dark shopping centre at three in the morning, holding a board up, thinking, this might be my last job like this.
S2.fieldNote: Her household has three exposures at once: her job, her husband's taxi and the tenant's rent. She copes by making lists and acting, starting with the estate agent. She sees her twenty-two years managing people as her way back into work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people take it seriously, and I'd tell my friends to start now. I'm not the type to make speeches about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be sixty-three, nearly done, and the house would be paid off. Pavel would have a few years to change track. It's not great, but it's manageable, if we plan it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the extra mortgage payments going and clear the house in two years. I'd pick up the new tools on site once they were proven and see if I could get into setting out or supervising. We'd decide about the flat in year three, depending on prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I could sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Pavel do with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push him to do a course, maybe as a driving instructor for the self-driving lorries, if that's a thing, I don't know. Or delivery, or care work driving old people. He'd grumble, but he's not stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'manageable'. What makes it manageable for you and not for others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paid-off house and the flat, honestly. Lots of the hotel girls have nothing behind them. I've been lucky and I've been careful, and I know the difference matters.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people take it seriously, and I'd tell friends to start now. I'm not the type for speeches.
S3.think: Honestly, I'd be sixty-three with the house paid and nearly done, and my husband would have time to change track. It's manageable if we plan it.
S3.do: Keeps overpaying the mortgage to clear the house within two years and adopts proven site tools, aiming for setting out or supervising. Decides about selling the rental flat in year three based on prices.
S3.quote: I've been lucky and I've been careful, and I know the difference matters.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Olga room to sequence decisions: house first, flat in year three, Pavel's course in between. She's honest that her comfort comes from both luck and care, and compares herself to former colleagues with nothing behind them. She'd move toward supervising rather than retraining from scratch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, there's no excuse not to be ready. I'd tell the young ones on site to think hard about their next step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be retired by then, so it's about Pavel and the kids. Ten years is enough for him to ease into something else or just retire with me. Honestly, I'd stop thinking about it after a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, get good at the joinery, finish at sixty-three or so, and keep the flat as our pension. I'd learn the new kit when it came, like I always do once someone else has tried it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A little uneasy about the flat and the tenant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if nobody has work, who pays rent? I don't know how that would work in ten years, and nobody does. But that's the one thing I'd keep an eye on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the young ones on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to look after the machines, not to fight them. And save something every month, even if it's a small amount. That's what kept me out of trouble.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty and there's no excuse not to be ready. I'd tell the young ones on site to think hard about their next step.
S4.think: For me, I'd be retired, so it's about my husband and kids. Ten years is enough for him to ease into something else or retire with me.
S4.do: Carries on, improves her joinery and plans to finish around sixty-three, keeping the rental flat as a pension. Learns new equipment when it arrives, once others have tried it.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a little unease about the flat and the tenant.
S4.quote: Because if nobody has work, who pays rent? I don't know how that would work in ten years, and nobody does.
S4.fieldNote: Her one open worry with ten years is a bigger question than her own job: who pays rent if nobody has work. She admits she doesn't know and nobody does. Her advice to younger workers mirrors her own habits of saving and adapting once proven.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Pavel and I would both be hit at once and the flat with us. What would help is a bit of money from government while people retrain, and firms being honest early, not doing the sums behind our backs like the hotel did.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people who'd manage the robots. I managed twenty-two women for twenty-two years. Somebody will have to manage the machines and the people around them, and I'd quite like that to be someone like me.

headlineQuote: Somebody will have to manage the machines and the people around them, and I'd quite like that to be someone like me.
portrait: Olga Nakamura is a 58-year-old junior on a night-shift fit-out crew building stud walls, ceilings and counters in shops and offices, after 22 years running hotel housekeeping until robot hoovers and app check-in cut her team. She and her husband Pavel, a taxi driver, have a nearly paid-off house and a rental flat. Practical and in the middle politically, she uses AI now and then and picks up tools once someone else has proved them. Her worry is spread across her husband's taxi, the tenant's rent and her own job, and she copes by making lists and timing decisions like when to sell the flat.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and her husband would both be hit at once, and the rental flat with them.
whatWouldHelp: Government money while people retrain, and employers being honest early instead of doing the sums behind workers' backs.
